a: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire was a gradual process spanning several centuries, traditionally dated to 476 CE when the last Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by the Germanic chieftain Odoacer. The causes were complex and multifaceted. Key factors include economic decline and inflation, as the empire's vast territorial expanse became too costly to administer and defend; political instability with frequent changes of emperors, civil wars, and corrupt governance; military pressures from barbarian invasions by tribes such as the Visigoths, Vandals, and Huns who crossed the Danube and Rhine frontiers; overreliance on barbarian mercenaries who were not loyal to Rome; the division of the empire into Western and Eastern halves by Diocletian, which weakened the west; and social decay including the decline of civic virtue and the rise of a wealthy elite that avoided taxes. The adoption of Christianity as the state religion also shifted focus away from traditional Roman values. The Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantine Empire) continued for another thousand years, demonstrating that the fall was primarily a Western phenomenon. The fall of Rome marked the end of ancient history and the beginning of the Middle Ages in Europe.
